fig1_h_and_u_vs_quality.svg: Saturated water at 10 bar (Table A-3) as it evaporates. Both enthalpy (enthalpy_from_quality) and internal energy (internal_energy_from_quality) are linear in the quality $x$ — the lever rule — but $h$ lies above $u$ by the flow work $pv$, and that gap grows from 1.1 kJ/kg in the saturated liquid to 194.4 kJ/kg in the saturated vapour, because the same kilogram now occupies 172 times the volume. Enthalpy is exactly the combination that already contains the work needed to push that volume across a boundary, which is why it, not $u$, appears in every control-volume balance.
fig2_constant_pressure_heat.svg: Boiling 2 kg of water at a fixed 10 bar. In a constant-pressure process the boundary work $p\,\Delta V$ exactly absorbs the $pv$ part of the enthalpy, so the energy balance reduces to $Q=m\,\Delta h=\Delta H$ (const_pressure_heat) with no work term left over — the heat can be read directly off an enthalpy table. Taking the charge from saturated liquid to saturated vapour costs 4031 kJ, all of it latent: the temperature never moves off $T_{sat}=179.9\,^\circ$C while this is happening.
